subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to interrupt, but the auditor general was auditor of every dollar of expenditure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: We have had that discussed before. Perhaps hon. members, who are interested, will look it up.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Exactly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have in my hand the act incorporating the Canadian Patriotic Fund. I would ask hon. members to listen to the preamble and see if its very words might not be suitably substituted for some of those which appear in the present measure which relates to the much larger problem of relief as it is in Canada at the present time. It reads:
WThereas it is desirable to provide a fund for the assistance in case of need, of the wives, children and dependent relatives of officers and men, residents of Canada, who, during the present war, may be on active service with the naval and military forces of the British Empire and Great Britian's allies; and whereas money is now being raised for the said purpose, and it is desirable to provide for the administration of the same:	Therefore His
Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows-
Then follow the several provisions of the act. I say that the previous administration had before it this example of an effective method of dealing with a great question of relief. I venture to say that if something similar to this method, the one recommended by the opposition in each of the past five years, had been followed by the government of the day, the problem of unemployment and relief would not be anywhere near its present proportions, and expenditures would not have been at all what they have been during the past five years.
Turning to one of the clauses in the act I find this:
3. The objects of the corporation shall be to collect, administer and distribute the fund hereinbefore mentioned for the assistance in case of need of the wives, children and dependent relatives of officers and men, residents of Canada, who, during the present war, may be on active service with the naval and military forces of the British Empire and Great Britain's allies.
I call the attention of the house to the words "collect, administer and distribute." Hon. gentlemen opposite have been taking exception to provisions of this measure which, in some particulars, may have to do with the administration of relief. Yet both houses of the parliament of Canada, with respect to much smaller sums of money, at a time of emergency found this a desirable and necessary method of procedure. The record of the fund and of its administration is evidence of the effectiveness of this method of dealing with a great expenditure of the kind.
Turning to clause 7 I find this:
7. The corporation shall, subject to the provisions of this act, pay, apply or distribute to the best of its judgment, in such manner, among the persons entitled to share therein, and in such amounts, as in the absolute and uncontrolled discretion of the corporation seems proper or advisable; and the corporation shall take such means as it thinks necessary or advisable to ascertain who are entitled to share in the said fund, and to what extent and in what manner the persons entitled will be relieved by the corporation.
Did the previous administration ever make a similar provision with respect to the expenditure of relief moneys? Hon. members may search the record and they will find nowhere any provision which gave to the government of Canada powers to ascertain who were entitled to share in the relief payments, and to what extent and in what manner persons so entitled should be relieved.
I submit we have in what I have cited sufficient, not only to justify this parliament in taking the steps proposed, but to brand it as neglectful of its duty if, in the face of this very obvious precedent and example of an efficient method of handling a great relief problem, it should fail so to do.
Section 10 reads as follows:
On and from the 31st day of December, 1914, the accounts of the corporation shall be audited by the Auditor General of Canada, and a report of such audit with such further statement as seems proper, shall be published as the corporation directs; and the said auditor, or his successor in office, shall be the auditor of the corporation.
Under the late administration what did we have by way of a report from the auditor general of Canada as to how expenditures had been made with respect to relief?

speechtext: My right hon. friend is saying that every account was audited.

Employment Commission-Mr. Mackenzie King

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Towards the close of the last parliament, the auditor general had a few officials of his department go into some municipalities to see how public moneys were being spent. They presented reports to this parliament which, had they been gone into in any detail, would have aroused the censure of the entire country against the administration. The reports evidenced the greatest laxity. They evidenced one kind of scandal after another just because there had not been the proper or necessary supervision.
Now, may I ask what my right hon. friend said when we suggested there should be a commission along the lines proposed? He said that it would be an insult to the provinces to have anything of the kind done My right hon. friend sought to have the country believe that, in suggesting a national commission to supervise the expenditure of federal moneys, we were trying to invade the jurisdiction of the provinces. He stated, when it was suggested that the expenditure of federal money should be audited in detail, traced down, so to speak, from federal sources, that it would be an insult to the provinces even to suggest anything of the kind.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I correct the right hon. gentleman?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: What I said was that when we paid money to the province and got their receipt for it in accordance with the arrangements made, we could not follow the money and have an audit made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My right hon. friend took great care to maintain the position that all he would do or seek to do, with respect to conserving public funds and seeing that they were economically administered and distributed, was to pay over lump sums to the provinces, inquire of the provinces as to whether or not they had received the money, and, when their receipt was given, say that, so far as the federal government was concerned, the transaction was ended. That is a straight statement of fact, and that is largely why we have such enormous sums expended in the last five years.
I wonder whether members of this house have any idea what is really represented by the sums of money already expended for relief. Perhaps a true perspective might be given if I draw the attention of the house to what in a given year the total expenditure of the Dominion of Canada amounts to. I am quite

right, I think, when I say that during the five years of my right hon. friend's administration S200,000,000, in round figures, was spent on relief and for the employment of those who were unemployed. This does not include either loans or guarantees which are still outstanding.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Does that include public
works?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, but not all public works; such public works as were undertaken to assist the provinces, but not public works provided for in special bills for the purpose of providing work-$200,000,000, as I say, in those five years. I have in my hand a statement by years of the receipts and expenditures of the Dominion of Canada. Those who are not familiar with them will perhaps be interested in knowing that $200,000.000, is more than the total expenditure of Canada in all branches of government in any single year prior to the fiscal year 1914-15, when Canada was in the war. That amount, spent alone for purposes of relief and providing work for the unemployed is, I repeat, more than the total expenditure of this dominion in any one year, prior to the fiscal year 1914-15. Will hon. members please give thought to that? Then consider that my right hon. friend says all expenditures on relief should be looked after by the Minister of Labour; that one minister should be responsible for all which relates to relief and unemployment ; that all the minister needs to enable him to perform the task is to engage one or two extra clerks or officials and have them make reports to him on different subjects. It all comes back, Mr. Speaker, to what I said to hon. gentlemen opposite, time and again, during the last parliament, that I did not think they even began to apprehend the magnitude of this problem, or to understand it at all. Had they ever comprehended its magnitude and what it was likely to amount to as the years went on, I cannot believe, for one minute, that they would have continued trying to deal with it through the agency of a single department of government.
My right hon. friend this afternoon gave a strong reason why that effort should not be attempted again. Having in mind what he believed to have been responsible for the breakdown of a former Minister of Labour, I often marvelled that he had continued the policy he did. Time and again he has made very touching reference to the late Senator Robertson having been a casualty of the depression. He was referring to the fact that the late Senator Robertson, as Minister of Labour, took this matter in hand when the problem

Employment Commission-Mr. Mackenzie King
of unemployment was developing, with the result, as we all know, that his life was really sacrificed through the strain and stress of the work and responsibility placed upon the shoulders of one man. Now, I ask members of this parliament: Do you wish to run the risk of a repetition of that sort of thing? The immediate successor of Senator Robertson as Minister of Labour left the problem pretty much alone. We never could get any information in this house from the last Minister of Labour of the late government on any aspect of the unemployment problem. When we sought to secure accurate statistical information, it was not available. The minister permitted the department and its work to slide along month after month, and year after year.
What I want to bring out at the moment is that anyone who understands this problem will realize that, no matter how able and efficient a minister may be, and how able and efficient his staff may be, no single department of government can begin to grapple with this question, as it has to be grappled with, in the light of its magnitude at the present time.
What was done at the time of the war as respects departments of government? They continued their regular work, but during the war the government of the day found it necessary to supplement their activities by establishing many commissions for one service after another. We had a purchasing commission, to make purchases necessary for war purposes. That work was not left to a single department of government. It was recognized that the whole business was so exceptional that the regular departments carrying on their ordinary work, even by extending their staffs, could not do, and were not suited for, the extraordinary demands of the war period. Then there was a food board established to deal with the matter of food supplies, a fuel board to deal with the supply of fuel, and a munitions board to deal with the purchase of munitions.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That was a British
commission.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
British, but
dealing with the purchase of munitions manufactured in Canada. During the period of the war there was a great demand for manufactured commodities. There was a great demand for foodstuffs. There was, as already mentioned, the National Patriotic Fund to look after the problem of relief. There was available sufficient money in circulation to give employment to everyone. And back of it all, there was the fervour and enthusiasm
of the people which had been raised to a high pitch of endeavour through appeals to patriotic purposes and aims. Yet, notwithstanding all this, the government of the day found it necessary to create additional bodies to carry on exceptional phases of the work connected with the war. To-day, when hundreds of thousands are unemployed, with little money in circulation, and when the countiy has passed through five years of depression, it is a very different thing altogether to get the several relief and other agencies of the nation working in cooperation on the problem of unemployment. The business of coordinating the national efforts in time of war is an easy task compared with that of coordinating efforts for providing relief and for supervising expenditures, in a time of great depression which has run on for year after year as this one has.
May I go a step further? The work of this commission falls largely into two main divisions, one which has to do more particularly with relief, and one which has to do more particularly with employment. I have mentioned how the parliament of the war period sought to deal with the question of relief. Let me now say a word about the question of providing employment.
Did the parliament of that day leave to the haphazard passing of orders in council, for all kinds of purposes, the provisions of ways and means to reestablish in civil life in this country the men who had been on active service overseas and who, as a consequence of their service abroad, found themselves out of employment when they returned? Did its members rely upon any existing department to get men back into employment? Did the Union government under Sir Robert Borden rely on the Department of Labour to reestablish in civil life those men who were without employment and who were returning from overseas, in numbers not at all comparable with the numbers of those out of employment to-day? What the government did was to create a new department of government altogether for purposes of reestablishment, organize a new department of government under a minister and deputy minister, to deal exclusively with the problem of reestablishing in civil life men who had served overseas.
I have before me a copy of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment Act. The act incorporating the Canadian Patriotic Fund, to which I have referred, was assented to on August 22, 1914, when the necessity of dealing with the great problem of relief arose at the beginning of the war. The Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment was created in
1782	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Mackenzie King
1918, just at the close of the war when the men were beginning to come back to Canada and needed assistance in reestablishing themselves in civil life. Section 2 of this act reads:
There shall be a department of the government of Canada to be called the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment over which the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment shall preside.
The minister shall hold office during pleasure, Hid shall have the management and direction af the department.
That department was created in spite of the fact that the Department of Labour was in existence at that very time.
Let me read one section of this bill. It will disclose that duties being assigned at the present time to the employment commission are not very different in some particulars from those which were assigned to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment. Power is given to make regulations covering hospitals, workshops and other institutions. The act further provides:
(e) for prescribing the payments, grants or allowances, if any, to be made to persons or their dependents whenever such persons are being cared for under the provisions of this
act, either by medical treatment, training or otherwise;
There are many sections I might quote, but I shall not take the time to do so now. The section I have read1 shows that it was found advisable to have a department to supervise grants being made to individuals. We in this parliament are making grants, not merely to individuals, but to provinces. We are making them, not in small sums but in millions and in hundreds of millions of dollars. But as yet there is no special department, there is no special agency, associated with the government, to supervise this vast expenditure of public money.
Let me repeat, at a time when the industries of the country were working at their maximum, when the demand for manufactured goods and the products of the farm was at its highest, when the whole country was organized for a vast national effort, it was found desirable and necessary to have two special enactments of parliament, one to deal with such relief as was necessary at that time, and the other to deal with the question of reestablishment, once the necessity for it arose. Surely after five years of experience, such as we have had in in this country during these years of depression, there is an obvious need for a body such as is proposed by this bill to deal with these two same problems of relief and re-establishment, which only under different conditions exist in infinitely greater 
magnitude to-day. The need is perfectly obvious.
The examples to which I just referred were repeatedly placed before the ministry of the day, but no heed was given to them. They wer-e subsequently in a general election placed before the country and the people of Canada approved them. With the problem what it is to-day, we cannot be too sure that even along with other measures, they will suffice to effect a solution, or that a solution will be achieved in the near future. We do believe, however, that, unless a step of this kind is taken, there will be no overtaking the problem at all.
I have very little comment to make with reference to what has been said by most hon. members in other parts of the house who are opposed to the government. Some have been critical towards the measure proposed by the government, I suppose because they feel it their duty to be critical. I have listened very carefully to the debate throughout. I have yet to discover a single suggestion from the other side of the house calculated to be helpful to the government in dealing with this great problem. A suggestion has been made by one group that socialism is the only cure. May I ask my hon. friends of that group-the member of the group who was perhaps foremost in putting forward the idea that something in the nature of a socialistic state was the only thing that would solve the unemployment problem has just come in-is it going to be possible, during the term of this parliament, to bring a socialist state into being? If it is not, wherein is it helpful to suggest that nothing short of the socialist state will solve the unemployment problem? Members of this house are here for a limited period of years to deal, among other things, with the problem of unemployment. The only suggestion that can be of value to the government or to the country during the next four or five years is something to which effect can be given during that period of time. Theories that proclaim, as an hon. member said this afternoon, something new and untried, cannot be helpful in the solution of our problems unless there is some prospect of their being put into effect within the next few years through the agency of this parliament. They must otherwise be treated as something put forward merely as a subject for academic discussion.
An exception I do take to criticism of some hon. gentlemen, is their assumption that this bill to establish a national employment commission is the government's entire program

Employment Commission-Mr. Mackenzie King
with respect to unemployment and relief. Some members have stated that, within the four corners of this bill, they cannot find a solution of the problem. My hon. friend, to whom I referred a moment ago, was one of those who said that very thing. I want to speak particularly to him because he is an older member of parliament, and knows better. He knows that he should not expect to find within the four corners of this bill the things which he has said he cannot find there. He knows very well that, if he had looked at the order paper, he would have found reference to other measures to be adopted for the purpose of providing relief and employment.
My hon. friend and other hon. members have said that they could not see any provision for money in this bill. Apparently that is all most hon. members are looking for, something that is going to lead to expenditures of vast sums of money. In the last five years a great deal of money has been spent, but parliament has had very little to say about the expenditure; it has practically all been spent under the blank cheque authority taken from parliament by the administration of the day. This government does not propose to proceed in that way. We propose, with respect to whatever moneys are to be spent, to ask parliament to appropriate the moneys for the specific purposes for which they are to be used. That is why there is nothing in the proposed enactments which this government has brought down in the nature of a 'blank cheque or blanket authority to legislate by order in council.
To appreciate aright the government's policy in dealing with relief and unemployment, there are three enactments which have to be considered together. There is, first, the one which relates to this national employment commission. Second, there is the one, to which I have just referred, which has to do with assistance in the relief of unemployment, the promoting of agricultural settlement and rehabilitation, and the development, conservation and improvement of certain natural and other resources. That bill we shall take up immediately we have concluded with this particular measure. Third, there is a supply bill in the form of special supplementary estimates, which will set forth the various projects for which the house will be asked to vote the necessary moneys. The government hopes to combine in one bill the amounts which will be required for these purposes over and above the sums required to meet the ordinary expenditures of government. We
do not propose to lessen the ordinary expenditures of government in any particular because indirectly they may have a bearing upon employment and relief. The various departments will make out their estimates in the usual way. In fact, they have done so already, and these estimates have been presented to parliament. Where, however, additional work is to be provided in connection with the various existing departments of government, or by means of grants to the provinces, or in connection with special public works or other activities, the details will be set forth in a supply bill which will enable hon. members and the country to see what the cost of reliei and the furnishing of work for the unemployed is likely to be in the course of the year.
I hope that the special supply bill will be brought down before the Easter recess. Perhaps I may say at once that, when it does come down, the total appropriation requested for purposes of relief and for providing employment will be seen to amount to over 850,000,000. Let me impress upon hon. members the significance of this sum. In doing so, I would ask hon. members which, in their opinion, is the correct course to follow with respect to the expenditure and the supervision of that vast sum of money, the one suggested by the leader of the opposition, or the one proposed by the government. The leader of the opposition and the hon. gentlemen who sit beside him advocate that the Minister of Labour should see to the proper supervision of the expenditure of these moneys; they contend that the department of Labour alone is all that is needed for the performance of this task. We maintain that, while all departments of government will have to do their full duty, there will have to be, in addition thereto, a body such as we propose to constitute; a National Employment Commission, which will survey and supervise the whole problem of unemployment and relief, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, as it relates not only to the expenditure of money by this government, but to expenditures by the provinces, the municipalities and private agencies as well.
To show what 850,000,000 really signifies, I should like to point out that the total expenditure of the dominion government for the fiscal year 1878, at the time Sir John A. Macdonald's government succeeded that of Alexander Mackenzie, amounted to a little over 830,000,000. When the Liberal government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into office in 1896 the total annual expenditure of the federal government was less than this sum of 850,000,000 which
17S4	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Mackenzie King
we propose as an extra or special supplementary estimate, exclusively to help deal with the problem of unemployment as it exists at the present time. In 1896 the total expenditure of the Dominion of Canada amounted to $44,000,000. Properly to administer and supervise that expenditure required the attention of all the departments, the auditor general and every agency of government. Now the leader of the opposition says: Let the Minister of Labour do it. If we desire to be totally indifferent to the expenditure of the money of the people, that is the method to follow. If, however, we have any sense of trusteeship whatever, the time has come when we must check up and see what is becoming of the moneys expended for these purposes. May I go a step farther. This $50,000,000 constitutes only the contribution of the federal government towards the solution of the problem. A corresponding amount, or something approximating it, will have to be paid out by the provinces as well as additional amounts by the municipalities. You cannot separate the three in estimating the cost to the country of relief in Canada to-day. The people of Canada have to pay the bill whether it is paid out of the moneys of the municipalities, of the provinces or of the dominion. The people of Canada will never know the cost of relief until there is some agency to bring together in one report the expenditures of all the agencies involved, government and private alike, nor will there be any substantial lessening in the amounts until they know the manner in which all the different agencies are supervising their expenditures and carrying out the works for which the expenditures are being made. That is one of the main purposes of this commission, and I venture to say that no agency other than a body such as we suggest can possibly carry it out.
Reference has been made to the powers and duties of the commission. Let me ask hon. members to look again at these powers and see whether, in the first place they are right, and whether in the second place, they could be properly carried out by any body other than the one I have named. Many hon. members have spoken as though the purpose of the commission were solely to gather statistics. It is not fair to make a statement of that kind; that is only one of its purposes. They have talked as though the commission will be there simply to study. If that is the only contribution to be made to the discussion it would, I submit, be much better if some members devoted their time to studying, instead of discussing,

the subject under consideration. Certainly the national registration and classification of persons on relief form but one of the duties of the commission. The Minister of Labour and his department have done a quite exceptional bit of work in showing, in the absence of any [DOT]satisfactory data during the past five years, that it is possible to get together statistics helpful to this parliament as well as to the provincial governments and the municipalities in. dealing with the problem. But the department has only begun to gather a fragment of what is necessary if we are to know the true effect and inwardness of the unemployment situation.
Take the second of the powers and duties of the commission as set forth:
Recommend to the minister conditions to be complied with by any province obtaining grants for relief purposes from the government of Canada.
Is it not advisable to have attached to the moneys that are being voted by this federal parliament conditions which shall govern their expenditure? How is it going to be possible to estimate accurately what the conditions should be unless you have some organization which has power to supervise the manner in which the various provinces expend the federal money which is granted to them? What can the Minister of Labour or any minister of the crown in Ottawa know of the manner in which expenditures are being made in the maritime provinces, in Quebec, in Ontario, in the prairie provinces, in British Columbia? It is impossible for any minister of the crown, or any department of the government here at Ottawa to undertake to secure that information. What is needed is a body, such as this commission will be, which will be comprised of representatives from different parts of Canada and which will have a staff organized for the purpose of securing full particulars with respect to these matters.
Take the next duty mentioned:
Recommend to the minister effective means of mobilizing the agencies for relief both state and voluntary, and so coordinating their work as to avoid overlapping and abuses, and to secure proper provision and auditing of expenditures of all moneys.
Are these not necessary and proper duties? If they are, is it possible to have them performed in a period of so-called emergency by any agency of government other than one such as it is proposed to constitute under this bill? A national commission will be in a position, not only to supervise the expenditure of federal moneys or relief, but to get in touch with all of the provinces, and where

Employment Commission-Mr. Mackenzie King
it is necessary, with municipalities as well, to inquire into their methods of administration and expenditure, and, as far as possible, draw up plans and suggestions which will enable the work to be effectively coordinated and supervised from one end of Canada to the other.
Then take the next:
Investigate and report upon proposals for the carrying out of programs of public works and other projects to aid in providing employment.
We have been voting money for public works for the last five years, but has there been any definite plan, any definite scheme? Has there been any effort to ascertain whether the federal government was duplicating the work of the provinces or municipalities, or whether the various projects were in accordance with the greatest needs of the municipality or the province or the dominion itself? There has been no concerted effort to see that the most effective use was being made of the moneys expended.
Take the next:
Recommend to the minister measures with respect to programs of public works and projects of the dominion, the provinces, the municipalities, and other agencies, intended to aid in providing employment in a manner which will serve to mobilize and coordinate their activities.
I come back again to the amount of money that has been spent by the federal government-8200,000,000 in the last five years. Repeat that for the provinces, another $200,000,000; and put down another $100,000,000, if you like, for the municipalities. That is something like $500,000,000. I think that is about 8400,000.000 less than was calculated by one hon. member as having been spent by these three agencies combined. Does any one say that, if there had been a national commission, which had carefully planned projects essential to the development of the country, with a great sum such as $500,000,000 at its disposal, we should not have had something to show in Canada, as a result of that expenditure, at the end of five years? But what have we to-day?
Can you point to any national program, anything in the nature of coordination of the work of the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities along useful and necessary lines? Where can you point to a program of work duly outlined which, all will admit, will have to be done at some time, and which might be done effectively to-day when public monejs are available for the purpose, and done in a manner which will not only serve to give employment but which will also
render to the state a service that is essential? You cannot do so, simply because we have not had the proper agency to formulate such a program.
Take the next provision:
Investigate and report to the minister on measures of cooperation with commercial and industrial groups in devising means under which provision may be made for the maintenance and increase of employment.
Is this great problem of furnishing employment and providing relief to be left for all time to the agency of the state alone? Are we to educate the people of this country- I am afraid that has already been done and for too long a time-to look exclusively to the state for employment or for relief? It is going to be a very serious business for this country if we go on in this way. Unless we discover private agencies which will help solve this problem, and unless we can coordinate their effort and bring it into relation with the efforts of the state, there will be no solution at any time of the unemployment problem.
Take the next:
Investigate and report to the minister upon plans for the establishment of an apprenticeship system in industry;
Investigate and report upon ways and means of providing employment for disabled persons, and cooperate with the veterans' assistance commission in its efforts to secure suitable employment for ex-soldiers.
I think I may leave those sections to speak for themselves.
Let me come to the next:
Recommend to the minister comprehensive measures constituting a long-range plan of national development which may be proceeded with or discontinued from time to time as conditions may determine.
Is that not a very desirable step? I heard an hon. member speak this afternoon of the advisability of a national plan. One phase of a national plan would be to have the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities enter at this time upon the execution of obviously essential national projects. This would not only effect the completion of the projects themselves, but provide honourable and remunerative employment to citizens of Canada who for the time being find it im possible to obtain employment in private industry.
Finally:
To take such steps with the approval of the minister to ensure such publicity as in the opinion of the commission may be necessary to enable it effectively to discharge its powers and duties.
1786	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Mackenzie King
I wonder what would be said of a department of the federal government, particularly the Department of Labour, if it were to attempt by means of publicity to bring to light obvious abuses, rackets, overlapping and the like with respect to public expenditures made by municipalities or by any of the provinces or by the dominion. And yet,, may I ask members of the house: Have the past five years not taught us the necessity of something of the kind if we are ever to overcome this problem of relief and unemployment? For my part, I cannot see how some of the abuses which have arisen are to be remedied except through the agency of publicity. We heard a good deal in the last session of parliament about the power of publicity to remedy evils. Certainly I have been one of those who have always thought that there were some evils which publicity is much more effective in curing than penalty. Particularly are social wrongs and social frauds in this category. It is not the business of a department of government which has its own work to do, to attempt this task. But the fact is some agency will have to attempt it if we are to secure a solution of this question.
These are all part of the powers and duties of the commission. I think I am right in saying that hon. members generally realize they are essential duties, which can be performed only by some supplementary agency, such as the one I have indicated.
In proposing the appointment of a national commission there is no attempt to find a substitute for the work of government departments. This body is not intended to relieve the government of any legitimate responsibility. The government will continue to have its responsibility with regard to the solution of the problem. The government departments will continue to carry on the work of administration just as largely as it can possibly be carried on. But the departments will have the benefit, and the government itself will have the benefit of getting, from a body such as this, advice and information which will be a helpful guide and which will prevent much in the way of overlapping and waste in the expenditure of public moneys.
Something was said this afternoon about the desirability of moneys being spent for housing, for reforestation and reclaiming of land, about the desirability of spending money to clear slums and the like, in addition to providing for the more usual type of public works. Well, that is the very kind of work this commission is intended to

further. In order that there may be no chance for anyone to assume or to say that this is an afterthought, as a result of the discussion, I should like to read to hon. members what I said over the radio in an address delivered on August 5 of last year, during the course of the general election campaign, as to the functions and duties of the proposed commission. I shall quote but a small part:
The program to which a national commission would be asked, by a Liberal government, especially to direct its attention, with a view to ensuring cooperative effort, would include necessary projects already commenced or previously undertaken, such as: essential public works, buildings and municipal improvements; the extension and improvement of highways, and the elimination of level crossings; the provision of airway facilities and ground services; large scale schemes of afforestation, aimed, amongst other things, at preventing those conditions of drought and soil drifting which follow upon the absence or wholesale destruction of tree life. Equally important is the preservation, in more ways than one, of what we now have of natural beauty itself and also of forest wealth.
I believe the country would welcome, above all else, a comprehensive scheme of urban and rural improvements. Such a scheme would appropriately include the clearance of slum areas, housing programs, the repair and painting of buildings and fences, both in the cities and the country; and, of scenic development, which would serve to make of Canada a country second to none for tourists, and to afford to the people as a whole fuller opportunities of recreation and the enjoyment of natural beauty. Indeed, all projects might readily be made to contribute to these ends. The interests of tourists and the enjoyment of our citizens generally could, for example, be promoted by making many a highway into a tree-way, and by making accessible, and improving the approaches, to areas of great natural beauty. The development of our national parks might well be supplemented by the creation of a larger number of smaller parks. Much of national importance might also be accomplished by the preservation of historic sites, residences and monuments, and the beautification of their surroundings.
All this could be worked out by the commission as part of a long-range scheme of national development, to be proceeded with or discontinued, from time to time, as conditions might determine. The employment which it would serve to create would be all in the nature of constructive work. Comprehensive measures of the kind would serve to increase the social capital of the country as distinct from its private capital. It would improve and beautify our country. Moreover, it is work which would appeal to the imagination, and which should arouse the interest and enthusiasm of those who may be assigned to it.
I submit that this is a constructive program of national development, in the truest sense

Employment Commission-Mr. Mackenzie King
of the word. We have to vote these vast sums of money; 850,000,000 will be voted in the course of a few days in this house. Why not spend that $50,000,000 in a manner which, while providing work for those who are unemployed, at the same time will create for the state great social assets as distinct from its private capital? Thousands of men, who are unemployed, owing to circumstances over which neither they nor the state itself have any control at present, may in this way, be made to feel that they are employed as citizens of the state and, in the truest sense of the word, are helping to build a greater Canada?
In order to emphasize the immediate necessity of a body such as this, I should like to direct attention to what has taken place in this city and in this province within the immediate past, if, indeed, not at the present time. Shortly after the administration came into office, with a view to helping the municipalities during the winter months, we increased the grants in aid to the provinces by seventy-five per cent for the months of December, January, February, and March. That was a rather large increase. We had to make the best estimate we could of the requirements of the situation. Fortunately a dominion-provincial conference had been held and we had been able to ascertain, at first hand from the premiers of the different provinces and the provincial treasurers and other members of their governments, what was necessary to enable them and the municipalities to meet their requirements during the winter months. In passing let	me not forget to say that the
complete answer to my right hon. friend's contention, that the provinces would not consent to any degree of federal supervision of relief activities, lies in the fact that every province in Canada endorsed the idea of a national commission and offered to cooperate with it when established. As I say, we had the advice, the information and the knowledge which came to us through the week's discussions on this question with the members of the governments of the different provinces. We subsequently increased the grants in aid by seventy-five per cent.
It would have been a very fortunate thing for all concerned had there been a national commission at work during the past few years, appointed if you like by my right hon. friend, to which we could have gone, before deciding what particular percentage of increase should have been made in the way of relief grants to the different provinces. When I say "we," I 12739-114
mean the federal government as the trustee of the people of Canada with respect to their moneys. We and the provinces would have been in a better position in deciding upon the adequate amounts, which are in the nature of trust funds, if there had been some body which could have given us advice on the actual situation, based upon information gathered from day to day and from month to month, to say nothing of from year to year. There was, however, no such body, and we had to do the best we could. I think we made, from the point of view of the federal government-I am speaking not of our government, but rather of this parliament-a very generous grant to the provinces. We made it clear, at the time, that the grant was for the purpose of meeting the situation in the winter months when there was bound to be less employment and more in the way of distress and need for relief than in other months of the year. We made it clear at the same time that the extra grant was for these four months only, and that at the end of the period we might have to revert to the previous arrangements. Some days ago the government was faced with the question of what it was wisest to do considering that the four months had nearly passed. Had we followed the course, indicated as a possibility, of reverting to the amount granted to the provinces, when we came into office, we would have notified them of a cut of seventy-five per cent. We discussed the matter for some time and concluded that, as we had not yet had an opportunity to give to some of these problems the study we should, and as we did not have a commission to advise us or any independent source of information, it would not be advisable to run the risk of making a cut which might embarrass the provinces or the municipalities. Instead, then, of making a cut of seventy-five per cent, or fifty per cent, or twenty-five per cent, we indicated that for the month of April there would be a cut of only fifteen per cent, and probably a further cut in a subsequent month.
To-day the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) asked a question of the government with respect to that fifteen per cent cut; it was, I think, as to whether or not the municipalities are to be allowed to suffer. We have received representations from one or two provincial governments to the effect that they are already embarrassed because there is a fifteen per cent cut. Who is to decide as between the municipalities, the provinces and ourselves as to what is right and just and fair in regard to such matters?

17S8	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Mackenzie King
It is not our money to do with as we please, but money which belongs to the people of this country, for whom we are trustees. You cannot leave a question of this magnitude to the Minister of Labour. You cannot leave it to any department of the federal government. It must be a part of the duties of a commission in which the provinces, municipalities and dominion alike will have reason to have confidence. They are all equally interested; the municipalities and the provinces, like the dominion government, are interested in avoiding waste of public money. They will be quick to recognize that a body such as the one proposed is the only kind of organization which can go in and effectively size up the situation.
That is what has happened to-day. A similar situation may arise every month, and possibly every month for one, two or three years, depending very much upon how the matter is handled in the meantime. Which course will bring us nearer a solution of the problem following the method which has been adopted in Canada for the last five years, namely leaving it to the attention of one minister of the crown, or taking the course we now propose, the establishment of an organization which can give information not only to parliament but to the provinces, municipalities, private agencies and the press?
Take the case of this very city of Ottawa: What have we heard in Ottawa during the winter? We have heard that a grant made to the province of Ontario to be passed on to the municipalities, had not been so passed on. The city of Ottawa has been complaining that it has not received what it should have received out of the increased federal grant. Who is to decide that question? Can the Minister of Labour settle it, as between city and province? Can any body connected with the federal government undertake that particular task? If a matter affecting municipal, provincial and dominion funds is to be dealt with satisfactorily, it is essential that the party who deals with it be above all, but not part of, any one of these particular entities. That is why we need a commission of this kind to assist in the distribution of outlays and in the supervision of expenditures.
I shall not take up more of the time of the house, but I hope I have made it clear that, in the course the government is pursuing, it is simply carrying out the policy whieh we advocated five years ago, and which we have advocated ever since, year in and year out in the House of Commons. That policy was

placed before the public in the general elections, and it received the endorsation of the people of Canada. It is a policy based not upon mere theory, but upon practice which has proved to be an effective and helpful method of administration of public funds in a time of great national emergency. Above all, the plan developed is one which, we believe, will help to solve the problem of unemployment and to meet the needs of relief. It is one which is essentially constructive in its bearing on many projects essential to the future needs of Canada. Whether it will succeed or not, no one can say; as a plan for effecting a nation-wide cooperative effort in providing employment and administering relief, it is as practical as anything which could possibly be suggested. The degree to which it will succeed will depend very largely upon the support it receives from hon. members in this chamber. The government will welcome all in the way of criticism so long as it is fair and just, but may I venture to suggest that each member of the House of Commons, in seeking to . aid in a solution of this emergency situation, in some ways the greatest with which this country has been faced at any time, and which may grow to proportions the like of which none of us can comprehend, will do well to realize that his first and chief obligation is to make constructive suggestions or to conclude that for the time .being at least it may be equally helpful to remain silent.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention, having been incapacitated for the greater part of the week, to take part in the debate, but after listening to the progress of the debate to-day I feel it my duty to say at least a few words concerning the measure.
I was sorry indeed to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggest that the measure introduced by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) had not received fair criticism and treatment from all quarters of the house. I do not think the Minister of Labour would say amen to a suggestion of that kind. I have listened to the debates which have taken place and that part of it which developed to-day, and I must say that as yet in this chamber I have never heard a debate carried on on a higher plane and with more constructive criticism or more sympathy for the measure as introduced than the debate to which I have listened to-day and which, during my absence, I followed in Hansard.	.

Employment Commission-Mr. Walsh
Before he took his seat the Prime Minister asked in what body the municipalities or provinces would have confidence if they did not have a commission of this kind. May I ask the right hon. gentleman whether the provinces or the municipalities have lost confidence in the present government? Is it necessary to establish a buffer state between the government and the municipalities and provinces in order to protect the government from the abuse which may follow legislation of this sort? I leave that question with other hon. members.
It is not my intention to assist in making the measure a political football, nor is it my intention to thrust into the political arena so important a problem. I decry any possibility of that kind. I am afraid, however, that as hon. members read and compare the speeches of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and the Prime Minister, they will readily see who is leading this great problem into the realm of politics and who is trying to keep it out of politics. It would be most unfortunate if this bill and the whole question of unemployment became a political issue, in the regular sense and meaning of the term. This would not do the country any good and certainly it would not ease matters for those who during the next few years may be dependent upon a measure of this kind.
During the course of his observations the Prime Minister mentioned other commissions which had been established in the past. I suggest to the house that the examples he used were those of commissions established to deal with matters pertaining to the federal field and the federal field only. The body set up to handle soldiers' civil reestablishment was handling a federal matter, and a separate and distinct department was built up to assist those thousands and thousands of men returning to Canada to reestablish themselves in this, their homeland. That was a federal matter and had nothing to do with the provinces or the municipalities. I suggest to the Prime Minister that the other examples to which he referred were of a similar kind and were not analogous to the commission under discussion.

speechtext:
I mean to say that the
problem of relief and unemployment is a matter belonging to the federal government, the provinces and the municipalities, and is quite different from the problem of civil 12739-lMJ
reestablishment of soldiers, which is altogether a federal matter.
I do not want the Minister of Labour or anyone else in this house to think for one minute that I am opposing this measure as such. I am in favour of any measure that is going to help us in any way to get out of the present depression, but there are certain features of this measure that I do not like. As I have mentioned already on many occasions in this chamber, I am radically opposed to the appointment of commissions. I am absolutely opposed to a commission form of government. To my mind we have already twice too many commissions. I am reminded by the remarks made by my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) when the estimates for the fisheries department were under consideration, and he described in his own inimitable way how the appointment of a snow-shoveler would very often lead to the creation of a department of snow shoveling. I suggest that this measure is another step of that sort. It is proposed that a commission handle this problem. Five years from now, Mr. Speaker, I venture to say that you will hardly recognize this commission that is to be appointed, for it will be surrounded by a staff greater, I dare say, than that which the minister now has under his command in the department. I am afraid of commissions; I do not like commissions. They have a peculiar way of building round themselves a sort of wall of protection behind which they smugly sit and compile figures and issue statements and booklets, and consider that they are doing a real man's job.
There is another feature of the debate I do not like, and the Prime Minister will excuse my taking exception to it, being a new member of this house. I do not like this constant reference to what has been or has not been done during the past five years.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
When I first entered this house, Mr. Speaker, there was naturally in
1790	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Walsh
the early part of the session much gloating over the victory that had been won in October, 1935. The reason for that victory was given during the early part of the session as being the immense popularity of the Prime Minister. The reason now given for the victory is the immense popularity of the employment commission that was promised to the electorate throughout this dominion. I assume we can take our choice as to why the election went as it did. I have it figured out in my own mind that no matter what government had been in power in the last five years they were due for a defeat, and a really good defeat. No government, be it Liberal or Conservative, could have gone through what this country had to go through for the five years from 1930 to 1935 and expect to receive approval from the electorate of the Dominion of Canada, and I suggest to this Liberal government, strongly entrenched as they are in power at the present time, that if they have to go through a similar period of depression to that which the Conservative government went through in the last five years they are going to meet the same Waterloo in 1939 or 1940.
We have heard in this house much reference to the causes of the depression and to the need for a measure of this kind. This measure is the suggestion of the Minister of Labour after looking at the situation as it now exists. I want to say in all fairness to him that I have read the speech he delivered on the second reading of this bill, and I do not think any hon. member could take exception to the remarks he made on that occasion. I think he is seriously making an effort to establish something that will help him solve this problem of unemployment. The only difference between the Minister of Labour and myself is that I have more confidence in him and his department, and in his ability to organize and reorganize his department, than he has himself. He wants to turn over the work of the Department of Labour in this particular field to a commission. As I look over the record of the Department of Labour prior to 1930 I hardly think it was an overworked department. I feel that the present Minister of Labour would be quite competent to handle this situation if he had not been tied by an election promise that had been made and that must be carried out. I feel that he could engage sufficiently competent assistants to render the establishment of this commission unnecessary, and in that way curb the expenditures that are bound to arise through a measure of this nature.
(Mr. Walsh.]
One can picture the appointments to this commission. Of course, the appointments are to be non-political. No politicians or nearpoliticians need apply. The commissioners are to be gathered together here in Ottawa; then they are going to proceed to collect statistics and compile and publish all that information, and then they are going to proceed to act upon it. Now, why could not that be done by officials in the Department of Labour? Why could there not be a committee formed in the department to do that self-same work, instead of adding to the burdens of the department by giving it another body with which to deal? The only reason I can see for the appointment of a commission of this kind is that it may act as a buffer state between the government and those who are seeking aid and relief in connection with unemployment m this dominion. That is the only reason I can see, and I do not like political manoeuvres and appointments of that sort. I think any government in power should take full, absolute and complete responsibility for their actions, and not place themselves in a position to say: We have nothing to do with the matter; here is the commission; you must go to them, and if they do not do as you would like them to dio, we are very sorry but we cannot assist you in any way; blame the commission; we have nothing to do with the matter; we did all we could but the commission would not act as we would like them to do.
I do not think the Minister of Labour when he was teaching-and by the way the Prime Minister did make me feel at home in the house to-night when he suggested that members should go back to their rooms and do a little studying before coming here to speak; he did make me feel that I was back in the lecture theatre and in the classroom once more-I do not think the Minister of Labour when he was propounding his economic theories and studying this question from the point of view of a professor of economics at Queen's university found the same solution for the problem as he is finding to-day as Minister of Labour. I think the solution he found as professor of economics at Queen's would be a better one to put into effect than the one that he is urging this house to adopt at the present time.
During the course of his remarks the Prime Minister suggested that the government in power during the past five years had done little or nothing; that they had done a tremendous amount of manoeuvring but actually had accomplished nothing; that they did

Employment Commission-Mr. Walsh
not even recognize the full significance of the condition as it existed. I do not think he was really sincere when he made that statement. I do not think any government would stay in power five years and treat * this question just as a paltry addition to the worries of government. There is no man in Canada, be he Liberal or Conservative; there is no member of this house who does not recognize the proportions of the problem with which we have to deal. When the Prime Minister suggests that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and his supporters did not realize the stupendous task that was ahead of them, I feel he is making a statement not borne out by the facts. The previous government did recognize the problem and they made a serious effort to combat it. That effort was not in line with what is suggested now, but it should not be suggested that they were un-Canadian enough to neglect the problem of unemployment and leave it to shift and drift to a possible conclusion by the coming in of better times. They did their work and did it well, and many members of that government broke down their health in their efforts to deal with the unemployment situation. They made mistakes, but who does not make mistakes? The only person who does not make a mistake is the one who sits back and does nothing. They made a lot of mistakes, but I do not mind seeing a man making mistakes if in the end he gets somewhere and accomplishes something. It is only by making mistakes that we get anywhere or accomplish anything in this world.
We cannot analyze the cause of this depression. It is no worse in Canada than it is anywhere else, and as far as I can see we are in a better position than that of most countries of the world. Our position is not as good at the present time as that of Great Britain, but it is better than that of most other countries. In my estimation something was done during the past five years. If it did not accomplish a great deal, it at least put us into the position in which we find ourselves to-day. That condition was not aggravated as it would have been had nothing been done. I do not want to suggest, as did the Prime Minister that the government of 1930-35 were responsible in any way for the depression. I do not want to suggest that the Liberal government from 1929-30 were responsible for the depression, although they did not recognize that it existed during those years. They were in no way to blame for it. To my mind the real cause of the depression is industry. I have tried to analyze this picture and as far as I can see, industry itself is to blame. We
enjoyed a tremendous period of expansion from 1921 to 1928 and the dividend and profit seekers are primarily responsible for the condition in which we find ourselves to-day. They took the soul out of business. There was a time when I could apprentice my boy to the corner grocery, when I could have him learn a trade and then start him up in a profitable business in some corner of a new suburb; at one time there were prospects for our .boys, but there are none to-day.
We must readjust our thinking to the conditions as we find them to-day. Great industries have taken the soul out of business. They have forgotten the human element. Just as we forget the human element in business, so did we plunge down and down into the depths of the depression until we found ourselves where we are to-day. If these profits which these people were making had been properly applied during the heyday of our commercial existence, we would not be talking about measures such as the one we have before us to-night. It is because of the exploitation of the commercial and industrial life of our country by many of the so-called financiers that we find ourselves in our present condition. They have taken the soul out of business. They have forgotten that which our forefathers knew when they established1 themselves in business fifty, sixty or a hundred* years ago; they have forgotten the import of that question which we hear so frequently in Sabbath sermons, "Am I my brother's keeper?" Too many business men have eliminated that thought from their code of ethics and the man who works in industry is now the forgotten quantity. The result is that he is bearing the load of the depression, not the business leaders and the financiers. As a result of the conditions that both governments have allowed to grow up around us the very life-blood has been sapped from the economic and industrial life of our communities.
As I said when I commenced my speech, I am not opposing this measure although I do' not agree with certain features in it. It will go through this house, but I assure the Minister of Labour that after it does go through, everything done by this commission will have my heartiest support. After this discussion is through I believe that all hon. members should get behind the Minister of Labour and give him their moral support. In standing by him we are standing by our country and we can help ourselves out of this depression by such an attitude. I want to emphasize again that this problem of unemployment should be kept out of the realm of politics. Once it gets into politics we are sunk. I want
Employment Commission

to leave that thought with the Minister of Labour. I am with him one hundred per cent, but I would rather he would strike out the clause appointing a commission and assume full responsibility himself. He could reorganize his department and do this work more effectively and more efficiently than any commission.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee on the bill, Mr. Ward in the chair.
Sections 1 and 2 agreed to.
On section 3-Commission constituted.

I can assure my hon. friend that these are the two considerations which shall guide us in selecting the personnel of the commission and these considerations obviously have a relation to the two problems that will confront the commission, the great problem of reemployment, which involves the closest kind of continuing cooperation with industry and commerce, and the problem of relief which is of a somewhat different order and which has never existed before in its present dimensions in this country.

thing to say in connection with the appointment of these commissioners, or will the municipalities or any organization other than simply the governor in council be consulted?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE

Clearly this is a matter which will have to be determined by the governor in council. This national employment commission is being set up not by legislation of the provinces but by legislation of the dominion parliament. It is designed to secure and, I trust, will secure, by virtue not of its personnel but of its functions, the cooperation of the provinces and the municipalities.

speechtext:
The Prime Minister indicated earlier this evening that the work which the government will require of this commission will be most varied, and one of its duties, I think I understood him to say, would be to discover the extent of the expenditures already incurred by provinces and municipalities throughout Canada. I was surprised to hear him say that, because I had supposed that in the minister's own department there was considerable, if not conclusive, evidence of what that expenditure was. What I would like to know is: In what way will this commission

Employment Commission
be in a better position to acquire that knowledge, if it is not now there, than would the officers of his department? During the past four or five years the minister's officials have travelled through the nine provinces of Canada and been in touch with each of the provincial governments. There have been dominion-provincial conferences continually; agreements have been arrived at between the dominion and the provinces; I am surprised that there is a lack of information in regard to work which is being carried on for this purpose throughout Canada, and I would like to know how the commission will be able to do what the department apparently has not been able to do.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not find among the functions of the commission that which has just been suggested by my hon. friend. The securing of such information might very well relate to some of the specific functions to be entrusted to the commission. It is quite true that the Department of Labour through the unemployment relief branch does receive information respecting expenditures in the various provinces, but I think I arn correct in saying that we have not complete and comprehensive information respecting the detail of expenditures in the provinces and municipalities. When the dominion government was contributing upon a pro rata basis of thirty-three and a third per cent to the provinces there was more occasion to obtain that information in detail, but since that policy was changed in 1934 to a system of grants in aid we are not in the same position to obtain information respecting expenditures by provinces and municipalities. It is obviously desirable that we should have that information; and that it should be placed before the national employment commission in its study of the feasibility of public works programs and where particular projects of public works might usefully be prosecuted.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I listened with great
interest to what was said by the hon. gentleman in that regard, as well as by the Prime Minister. The difficulty is this:	Does a
commission set up under the circumstances indicated in this measure hope to be able to displace the elected representatives of the people in a municipality? If the municipality elects a mayor and board of aldermen and sanctions expenditures, and assistance is given to it by the dominion through the province, is it suggested that the commission is to analyze those expenditures? That is what the last observation of the hon. gentleman would lead one to conclude. If his statement
is to be taken in the terms in which it is made this commission is really to displace the representatives of the electors of the community in determining the desirability of expenditures in that locality. It means that if it means anything.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Certainly I had no intention of leaving that impression. What I intended to say, and what I think I did say, is that it would be desirable that this national employment commission should assemble information respecting expenditures upon relief works by municipalities and provinces throughout the dominion, and that the assembling of that information has an obvious relationship to the study and investigation of further programs of public works to which the dominion government might be asked to contribute. That is all I had in mind.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
But that has always been done. As long as there was undertaken by a municipality a public work to which the dominion contributed, under the terms of the agreement made with the provinces the vouchers were actually filed with the province for those expenditures, and the province in turn sent the vouchers to Ottawa. I explained the other day that there was not a single payment that ever left the auditor generals' office under the relief acts that did not carry pre-audit with two initials on it of the auditor's own staff, and the signature of some person representing the provincial government and that of some person representing the municipality. All that information is available here. Whether it is all sorted and sifted out I cannot say, but I know the report made by the ministers preceding the hon. gentleman indicated the expenditures made by the municipalities and provinces and the extent of the contribution by this government. But it was believed, rightly or wrongly, by the provincial representatives-I emphasize that -that that form of dealing with these matters was not the best, having regard to their limited financial resources, and therefore grants in aid were made which were indeed continued by the present government, and increased by seventy-five per cent as the Prime Minister said. The provinces then undertook the allocation of these moneys to the communities in question, and the communities in question were responsible to the provincial authorities for the expenditures thus authorized and for the allocations made. That information is and has been open to the minister. As a matter of fact the bureau of statistics also receives full information in respect to these matters. It wifi be remembered that under the act relating to the bureau of statistics they have
Employment Commission

wide powers, and they kept closely in touch with the municipalities for the purpose of obtaining information in respect to these matters. What gives me concern is: What is the commission going to do that is not already being done and has been done during the years past so long as expenditures went on by joint effort of municipalities, provinces and the dominion, or sums were granted by the dominion to the provinces, to enable them to carry on works and undertakings productive of employment?
Take for instance the matter of level crossings, or subways to overcome the danger of level crossings. That was dealt with by special provision at the last session of parliament, in addition to what had been done previously. It was found, of course, that the number of people employed in such undertakings was much smaller than it was believed would be the case, and on the basis of the reports received no effort was made to expand that class of work because it did not give employment to a sufficient number of people having regard to the great expenditure involved. In Hamilton, for example, and in other places the conditions to which I have referred were encountered, and were in part being dealt with under a statute passed by this parliament many years ago, whereby a sum of money was set aside to deal with the level crossing danger and appropriations were made available through the railway commission to assist municipalities to deal with the problem. Now, I cannot see that the commission is to add anything to that situation with respect to expenditures on public works carried out by the municipalities.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I sought to make it clear a moment ago that when the dominion government was contributing thirty-three and a third per cent of the total relief expenditures, the provinces thirty-three and a third per cent, and the municipalities thirty-three and a third per cent, there was an obvious necessity for our obtaining complete information respecting provincial and municipal expenditures.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is done by the department now.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes; it is there available, but since the change from a percentage contribution to grants in aid there has not been the same necessity for obtaining that information. I suggested that it was obviously desirable that that information should be collected and analyzed by a national employment commission in connection with its study of relief works and its examination of the utility of particular types of works in relation to employment and so on.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Surely any province that comes to the dominion for a grant of money would not withhold from the minister any information for which he might ask. If it did, the minister could very easily deal with the situation; the grant would not be made. As long as parliament makes a grant in aid it may ask for the fulfilment of any conditions it likes in connection with that grant. The provinces are just as much interested as is the dominion; I am sure that if asked for information they would readily furnish it, and if they did not the remedy is in the hands of the dominion.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Quite so.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Then, why have a commission to go out and collect such information?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me to remind him, there is in the functions entrusted to the commission nothing which relates to the collection of this particular type of information. The point has come into debate incidentally, as it were. I have tried to afford an explanation with the information now available, and have tried to indicate the value attached to the securing of the information.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I did not grasp the significance of the answer made by the minister to the question asked by the leader of the opposition in reference to subways.

speechtext: I do not think I gave any answer to that question.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE

speechtext: I am aware of that, but I did not get the minister's reply. I now understand that he did not make one. In view of that fact, can he tell the committee how the commission will take on a subway problem now handled by the railway commissioners, who deal with subways?

I do not think any one will question the fact that from the standpoint of social utility much can be said for increasing

Employment Commission
the number of subways and the avoidance of level crossings. There is in the bill, however, no suggestion that the national employment commission would in future deal with the expenditure of such funds.
