subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Then I should like to ask the Prime Minister to what he was referring when he suggested, if I understood him correctly, that the commission would have something to do with the elimination of level crossings.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I think the minister has made it quite clear that so far as the government is concerned, it will continue to do the class of work it has done in the past. The commission in making its surveys of all the work being done throughout the dominion will take account of what the dominion is doing, what the provinces are doing and what the municipalities are doing. It will seek to coordinate that work. As the minister has just indicated, in connection with a project such as the elimination of level crossings the commission might deem it advisable to emphasize the necessity for increasing that phase of the work and restricting work in some other direction. It might suggest that the use of an equivalent amount of money in some other particular manner might be more profitable. In its functions the commission will be advisory and supervisory, rather than administrative. Here and there in connection with its work there may be administrative functions which it might be obviously desirable to have discharged by the commission. Enough power is being given under the measure to permit of this-but not to enable the whole business of relief to be carried on by order in council, as the leader of the opposition would have hon. members believe. The commission may be granted administrative powers to a limited extent and in the circumstances I believe this will appeal to the committee as being reasonable.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The minister said something
about labour being represented on the commission, but I did not hear his observations fully. Will labour be represented on the commission?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: My statement was that we were fully aware of the interest of organized labour in the national employment commission, and we are giving careful consideration to the suggestion that a representative of organized labour should become a member of the commission.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Will the minister agree with me when I state that no class in the country is as greatly interested in the operation of the commission as are the working men.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: In what I said this evening I tried to make that very clear.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Will farmers be represented on the commission?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As the hon. member is
aware, at the present time the general problem of relief includes relief in the dried out areas in western Canada and in addition, as hon. members will recall, a considerable number of farmers on relief in other provinces. In selecting the personnel of the commission I said that we would have regard for geographical and occupational considerations, and on both grounds I should think it probable that the farming population would be represented on the commission.
There is, however, a special organization, concerned exclusively with farming problems, operating in the rehabilitation area. It may be contended that the whole question of agricultural relief is for the time being at any rate an aspect of the larger relief problem. If I may mention the matter here, when I spoke on the second reading of the bill I had intended to segregate the problem of farm relief. I think we ought to recognize that it has certain features peculiar to it. In the strict sense of the term, conditions in agriculture are not due to industrial dislocation. One might say that in the main these conditions are due to a series of droughts in western Canada.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: And soil erosion.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, and soil erosion. We are justified at any rate in stating that they are due to climatic disturbances or causes quite distinct from those which operate to produce industrial unemployment. For that reason we may hope that this portion, of the problem may be liquidated even before we are able to make as great progress with the industrial phase of the relief problem.
I believe I understand the interest of the hon. member in the agriculture aspect of the larger problem of relief and unemployment. Some one has said quite properly that one cannot very well speak of the people in the dried out areas as being unemployed. In the strict sense of the term they are not unemployed.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: They are just idle.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Well, I would not even
say that they are idle, certainly not at this season of the year.
Employment Commission

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is the government carrying on in the western dried out areas the conservation plan as outlined by the late government?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, that is being proceeded with.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I readily understand that it is impossible to have all parts of the country and all sections of the community represented on the commission of seven, but I should like to urge that in some way special attention be given to having actual representation of the large number of people now unemployed. I do not know how that can best be effected. In almost every province there are unemployed associations. I think in some way the commission should undertake to see to it that the actual needs of those unemployed are given careful consideration. It is one thing to speak from the standpoint of a large industrialist or some of our leading commercial men, but it is another thing to speak from the experience of the actual struggles of the unemployed, and the people on relief. That aspect of the matter ought to receive careful consideration.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Under section 3 subsection 1 we are evidently going to have a sort of glorified cabinet, to start off with. When we think of the 130,000,000 people on the other side of the line with only one relief administrator, Mr. Hopkins, for all the states in that great union, we realize that we are starting off very badly, in a year of economy, when we proceed to appoint seven commissioners. For arbitrations, only three commissioners are required, and that is ample. We do not want a glorified supreme court travelling all over this country. What sort of example of economy would it be to the unemployed to hire seven commissioners when three are enough? The more I study this bill the more it seems to me to be purely academic. It will create no jobs and give no relief. There will be a chairman appointed, a vicechairman, and I suppose, a deputy chairman. Just wait till you see it next year. Just wait till you see how this commission has grown and branched out in every province. This is one way to create jobs all right, for seven commissioners and a large staff, while the unemployed are walking the streets to-day still looking for jobs with the first of May coming on. Why, in Toronto the administration of relief for the whole city of 650,000 people is in the hands of one man. He runs the whole thing, reports to the board of control and council, and they give him the 
money. If one man can run the whole business of relief in a city of that size, why do we need seven commissioners? We are commissioned to death. It would be far better to appoint only one commissioner, but with seven commissioners we shall have them sitting round a table like a board of directors; there will be voting, and the majority are going to rule. I fail to see how the government can justify this expenditure.
In the old country some of their most important work is entrusted to one man. In this country we had one man operating the whole of the Canadian National Railways from coast to coast, and the ocean services as well, but to hand out relief on standard specifications we must have a glorified supreme court passing votes of so much money for coal, so much for this and so much for that, and I suppose the provinces and the municipalities will have their branches of the commission too. It looks to me as if the constitution of Canada was being turned upside down. The more I study this problem the more I am convinced that it would be better to appoint one man, instead of seven commissioners who will sit round a table like the directors of the Canada Life or of some bank. We would get better administration and greater economy if we appointed one man instead of seven, who will be Liberals, first, last and all the time.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am surprised at the remarks of hon. gentlemen opposite, including the hon. gentleman whom I spent most of my time complimenting the other night, and I am going to compliment him again to-night because I said that I would do so the next time I spoke. Hon. gentlemen opposite are assuming with regard to this legislation a role which is not quite becoming.
I have in my hand the expenditures in my own constituency of Halifax for the year 1934-35, and I am amazed-indeed, if that word could be magnified a thousand times it could not express my feelings at what I see in this report-and I am going to ask a question of the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) who has been interjecting remarks and suggestions as to the personnel of this commission. The Minister of Labour stated that the commission would be composed of representatives of industry and labour and those best acquainted with problems of unemployment and industry to help the government and parliament in putting people back into employment.
As I was saying, the expenditures to which I referred were for the year 1934-35 in my constituency. Everybody knows that it was

Employment Commission
thought that the election would be brought on in 1934 or early in 1935, and when the election finally came on, it was very much like the election that was brought on in 1896, when the bell of Canada had to ring and that gentleman who has passed to that bourne from which no traveller returns, Sir Charles Tupper, had to leave this chamber because, under the constitution, parliament had automatically dissolved, so he walked out and met his Waterloo at the hands of the people and Sir Wilfrid Laurier succeeded him as Prime Minister. On October 14 last the leader of the Liberal party (Mr. Mackenzie King) came in as Prime Minister of this country, and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), for whom I have the greatest respect, took in this house the seat that was formerly occupied by the present Prime Minister.
Turning to this report for the year 1934-35, I find that $1,182,000 was spent in the constituency of Halifax.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I must
call the hon. member to order. We are dealing with subsection 1 of section 3 of the bill.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, very considerable latitude was allowed to hon. gentlemen opposite, but I will put what I have to say in the form of a question to the ex-Minister of Public Works. I find by this report that there was paid to a gentleman, an architect, in Halifax, out of relief money that was voted by this parliament for the purpose of giving relief to the unemployed, no less a sum than $30,516.65. The people of Halifax, of Nova Scotia and of Canada, I am sure, would be amazed that an architect should receive that amount out of moneys voted for relief. I ask what he did to earn that $30,000 when there were homes in which there was not a bushel of coal and not a fire burning, in which children had to remain in their beds to keep warm, and in which people had hardly enough to eat. If hon. gentlemen opposite mean what they say, and they want to keep commissions from being of a political character, surely they should have practised when in office what they are preaching to-day. The present Prime Minister entered the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier as Minister of Labour; his life has been devoted to the welfare of the working classes, and if he had been in office I do not think this sum of $30,000 would have been paid out of relief moneys to an architect for his services in one year. I would like to know what he did to earn this amount. Prior to March 21 this architect
was paid $30,516.55, and there has not been that much money spent on the public building in Halifax over which he had control. One must come into court with clean hands, and hon. members opposite should remember this when they criticize the Minister of Labour and the government for their attempts to deal with this gigantic problem. The Prime Minister has been honest enough to tell the house that it may be next year, the year following or even four years before the country will be able to get out of this dilemma. When the leader of the opposition and hon. gentlemen associated with him assume that they are the trustees of the public treasury of this country, I ask them how they can justify that assumption when about $10,000 was spent in a little hole in a port about sixteen miles from Dartmouth to take out a few boulders. This is implemented and supplemented by item after item of expenditure on the eve of the election.
I will go even further and say that not one person who needed food or fuel in his home was put to work. Any man given work was put on solely because he was a Tory and because he and his friends were going to support hon,. gentlemen opposite. I would not have made this Statement to-night had it not been for the continuous attack on the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour. As far as the Prime Minister is concerned, he has a good memory, but he did not go quite so far as my hon. friend who the other day paid me a compliment, whioh I return to-night, as promised.
These figures amount to $1,182,030.56 and they are available to any hon. member who desires them. If that .money had been honestly expended or given to the people in Halifax city and county who really needed it, it would have more than taken care of all the distress of all people, irrespective of party, in Halifax county. There was as much distress when they were through spending as there was before. If this is true, I ask hon. gentlemen opposite whether they are serious in their criticism? Are they fair to a government that is desirous of doing its duty to the people, of carrying out its public trust? It has been asked whether politics are to enter into this question. I submit that in connection with these items nothing but politics entered into the matter. The cheques were issued by those who were in politics and in charge of the great spending departments of this country.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Halifax (Mr. Finn) has wandered a bit afield from the section we are discussing. He has delivered a sort of mild lecture-

speechtext: Too mild.

speechtext:
-as to their rights and
privileges. He seems to be objecting to expenditures that were made in the county of Halifax under the Public Works Construction Act. I do not know to what he is referring but-
Mr. FINN; I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend, but I want to say that these architect's fees were paid in connection with the federal building being built in Halifax. So far there are only a few pieces of iron sticking up and looking at the sky. Nobody could get work on that building unless he was a good Tory. I put several Conservatives on and I have been blamed for doing so.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for the information because it gives me something with which to start. He objects to the expenditure of $30,000 for architect's fees in connection with a very fine public building to be erected in the city of Halifax.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That has not yet been completed, but the fees are paid..

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Before you start a building you generally have the plans completed. Owing to the slackness in the construction industry architects' associations all over the country made representations to the late government that they were suffering from unemployment.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: They certainly stopped suffering when they got that.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The policy was adopted- I want to know if my hon. friend objects to it-of commissioning architects in different parts of the dominion to prepare plans instead of having them prepared here in Ottawa by the staff. In this way employment was furnished and relief was given to that particular type of unemployment. The commission allowed to this architect was less than the standard commission allowed by the architects' associations. As I recollect it, the commission was five per cent. When you employ an architect to design a building the size of the public building in Halifax, the money paid in fees does not all go to one man. He must have a staff of draughtsmen, and I venture to say that from twenty-five to thirty people were given employment in connection with the preparation of those plans. My hon. friend makes some-complaint in connection with em-

ployment, but let me say to him that tenders were invited and the contract awarded to the lowest tenderer.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: To the Foundation Company of Montreal.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not recall.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The hon. member does not recall? I will remind him that Mr. Victor Drury is a Tory and a great friend of the former Prime Minister, who, I see, has left the chamber.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is all right, but the firm that got it was the lowest tenderer. That is what I am saying and I ask my hon. friend whether he claims that any other course should be followed.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: No. The former Minister of Public Works has asked me a question and I will answer him by asking him why he authorized and paid $30,000 when the building was hardly started. If Mr. Dumaresq were to drop dead to-morrow, from what source would the money be returned?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: All I have to say to my hon. friend is that plans are prepared before a building is started and the architect is entitled to a certain proportion of his fees as the work progresses. Whatever amount he was paid he earned and was entitled to on the basis of his contract. If anything happened to him his plans and specifications would be available and the work he did would not perish with him. I cannot understand, therefore, what the hon. gentleman is driving at.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I assume that this commission will be appointed regardless of anything I may say. I am absolutely opposed to a commission because I dread another spendu ing department. However, we are in the minority and I suppose we have to submit; we cannot do any more kicking. But I certainly. always dread further expenditures in connection with salaries and that sort of thing. Has the minister considered what percentage of the money that is to be voted for relief will be used in administration, investigations, travelling expenses and so on. I know something about the welfare department in Toronto and the number of investigators and I know that every now and then some unnecessary person is appointed. I am afraid that the situation will be the same in this case. I hope that economy will be studied everywhere if the commission is appointed. I am afraid that a large percentage of the money that should go to relief will be used to employ people who do not need employment.

Employment Commission

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I appreciate the importance of my hon. friend's observations. It would be impossible in advance for me to give an estimate of the proportion which the expenditures of this commission would bear to the total expenditures made by the dominion for relief purposes. I recollect that an answer was given to a question some weeks ago indicating that so far as administrative expenses of the Department of Labour are concerned they bear an exceedingly small relationship to the total expenditures on relief. I fully understand the importance of economy in connection with the commission, and I realize the danger of setting up a self-perpetuating and self-expanding organization. This government takes the responsibility for recommending this means of dealing with the unemployment problem and obviously we must also take the responsibility for the expenditures incurred in relation to the results obtained.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Will the commission have power to initiate expenditures?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Any expenditures in connection with the commission must be approved by the governor in council, and the amount made available for the administration of the commission will be included in the special supplementary estimates to be passed by parliament.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am not referring particularly to the administration of the commission; I am referring to any expenditures that might be incurred in connection with public works. I understood from what the Prime Minister said that the commission would not have such a power, and therefore the statements made by some hon. members are evidently not well founded, because if the commission has no right to expend public funds it cannot become a spending body in the narrow sense of the word; it is more or less an advisory body to make recommendations. The cabinet in the final analysis and parliament subsequently will, I assume, be responsible for all expenditures incurred in relief.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Beaubier) referred to another commission appointed a short time ago, a conservation commission, of which I understand a former member of parliament has been appointed chairman, to deal with conservation in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta. In what way will this employment commission Cooperate with the commission referred to by the hon. member for Brandon?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The minister has asked me to answer that question in view of the fact that the work referred to is being conducted under the Department of Agriculture. The committee that was established last year, which might be regarded as a form of commission, is being done away with and the matter is now to be administered under Mr. Vallanee, as indicated a moment ago. We are cutting down the staff for the very reason mentioned by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence). The overhead costs were so great under the system set up that we have decided to cut down considerably on the staff to see that more money shall go to expenditure on the land itself rather than to office upkeep.
Mr. MacNICOL. I endorse anything in that direction, but I should like to know how the employment commission will cooperate with the committee to which the Minister of Agriculture has just referred.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The employment commission will have under its supervision all aspects of relief work throughout the country and will seek to coordinate these activities, whether they are under one department or another. As it happens, this work that is being done in the rehabilitation area is under the Department of Agriculture and not the Department of Labour.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is a point that
has given me great concern since this bill was introduced, namely, possible duplication. On the one hand we have an employment commission and on the other we have a committee or commission in connection with rehabilitation in the western provinces. If the latter is going to have a staff and the former as well is going to have a staff, then we shall be faced with the very situation that I have been fearing right along, namely, duplication.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The rehabilitation work is.not relief work in the strict sense. It is a matter of re-seeding lands that have been blown out, and providing water in places where dams can be constructed. It is not relief work in the sense that has been suggested; it is simply to assist farmers in reestablishing themselves on lands that have been affected in recent years by drought.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I understood that the
employment commission would have some connection with the work to which the Minister of Agriculture has referred.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
All these have to be coordinated.
Employment Commission

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is not relief in the strict sense of the word. At the same time we do include among those who are on relief those who are in the dried-out areas, but that by no means exhausts the number of farmers who are on relief in this country. In other words, the work done under the rehabilitation act does not of itself provide relief for all farmers throughout Canada. It is confined to a very particular area of the country. But inasmuch as it is a part of the larger problem it might very well be considered by the national employment commission, but not in an administrative way at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I submit that in the discussion we have more than covered the section; we have pretty nearly covered the bill.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There was one word in subsection 3 to which I wish to draw attention:
The commissioners may be paid such fees or compensation for their services-
Fees to a commission? Would not a salary or compensation be better than fees?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I think that "salary" suggests a good deal more in the way of permanency than "fees." An hon. member was suggesting that the commission might last for years to come. It is the hope of the government that it will not be necessary to have the commission continue for long, and for that reason I believe the word "fees" was thought to be more appropriate than "salary." It did not suggest the note of permanency which "salary" does.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The question I wanted to ask with regard to this is: Will the~e commissioners be employed during their whole time; and if that be so or if it be not so, in what way will the fees be made proportional to the services they render?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: My hon. friend has touched on a point which the government had very much in mind. It may not be possible to get the full time services of some persons we may hope to have as commissioners. In that event a fee will have to be arranged. Certainly in every case regard will be had for ability and the other circumstances which should govern the matter of retaining the services of whoever may be appointed.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Not necessarily residents of Ottawa then?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, no, not necessarily residents of Ottawa.

Section agreed to.
Seotion 4 agreed to.

On section 5-Secretary.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question on this section. It says that there shall be a secretary of the commission. On a work of the magnitude that apparently the commissioners are going to undertake it would look to me necessary to have two secretaries, one French speaking and one English speaking. If there was only one, it would be necessary to have either a French speaking or an English speaking one.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I move the following addition to section 5, to add subsection (3):
(3) Notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, chapter 22 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, the Civil Service Superannuation Act, chapter 24 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, or any other act of the parliament of Canada, a civil servant who, at the time of his appointment or employment under or pursuant the provisions of this act, is a contributor under the provisions of the Civil Service Superannuation Act, shall continue to be a contributor under the said act; his service under this act shall be counted as service in the civil service for the purposes of the Civil Service Superannuation Act, and he, his widow and children or other dependents if any, shall be eligible to receive the respective allowances or gratuities provided by the said act; and in the event of his being retired from his office or position under this act for any reason other than that of misconduct, he shall be eligible for reappointment in the civil service or to receive the same benefits under the Civil Service Superannuation Act as if his office or position has been abolished.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Before the amendment
carries I offer this suggestion to the minister, that in such sections of bills that are now coming before the house provision be made to maintain the preference formerly extended to ex-service men under the Civil Service Act. I notice that in the wording of a similar section of the National Harbours Board bill and other bills before the house no attempt has been made to carry out the preference, although when certain post offices were removed from the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Act it was expressly stipulated in the legislation then enacted that the preference formerly enacted would be maintained in appointments to the staff, and I think that in appointments to a staff of this kind the same preference should be maintained as was formerly granted ex-service men under the Civil Service Act. May I have an opinion from the minister on that question?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The amendment was
designed to deal with a somewhat difficult problem which confronted us in providing for the possible staff whieh would be employed by this commission. We desired to

Railways and Shipping
make it possible to use those who are at present in the civil service, and in order to effect that end the proposed amendment has been added. The form is precisely the same as that which was used in the National Harbours Board bill.
So far as the specific point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Mac-Neil) is concerned, I am not aware that with regard to temporary employees, to which this refers, the usual civil service preference for returned soldiers has been followed in past years. It is certain that we shall not be through to-night, and I shall be glad to look into that matter and give an answer when we meet again oh Monday.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Do I understand that these employees are chosen by the civil service commission?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: They are not?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No. The amendment was
designed simply to permit the transfer to the national employment commission, so far as we desire to do so, of those who are at present in the civil service.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOB NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That raises the whole
question as to whether appointments to this staff should be made by the civil service commission, or by the governor in council as proposed in this bill, and a great deal may be said on both sides of the question. I know some members want to say something on it, and I suggest that the committee rise, as it is eleven o'clock.
Progress reported.
